Christ's place above every power supports the hearers' received hope

Verse 16 says all things were created through the Son. It lists them: things in heaven and on earth, thrones and powers. Verse 20 uses the same range for reconciliation. God reconciles all things, on earth and in the heavens. The means is stated without softening: peace through the blood of his cross. Verses 21–22 apply it to the readers. They were once alienated, and now he has reconciled them.
The joined body grows through its head rather than added claims to special wisdom

Verse 18 describes a person who would rob the readers of their prize. He insists on false humility and the worship of angels. Verse 19 names what is wrong with him. He does not hold firmly to the Head. The body grows only from there, and the growth is God’s. Verse 10 has already said the readers are made full in Christ. So verses 20–23 ask why they submit to added rules.
Received new life requires changed speech and care within still unequal households

Verses 8–9 use the picture of clothing: put away anger, malice, and lying. Verse 10 says they have put on the new man. Verse 12 tells them what the new clothing is. It first names who they are: God’s chosen ones, holy and beloved. The five garments all concern other people: compassion, kindness, lowliness, humility, and perseverance. Verse 13 adds forgiving one another as Christ forgave. Verse 14 puts love over all of it as the bond.
Letters, messengers, and prayer connect separate assemblies with the chained speaker

Paul cannot visit; he is in chains (verses 3 and 18). The letter stands in for him, and people carry it. Verses 7–9 send Tychicus and Onesimus to tell what the letter does not. Verse 16 then orders two public readings. This letter is to be read at Colossae and at Laodicea. A letter from Laodicea is to be read at Colossae in exchange. The verse shows these letters were written to be heard by whole assemblies.
